newsitem.title: USA: Waco takes center stage at Oklahoma bombing trial.
newsitem.headline: Waco takes center stage at Oklahoma bombing trial.

text.p: Defence attorneys trying to save the life of convicted Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh portrayed him on Tuesday as deeply troubled by the government's raid on the Branch Davidian cult in Waco, Texas.

Using magazine articles, a videotape and a song, McVeigh's attorneys attempted to show jurors that the Gulf War veteran became distraught over the 1993 deaths at Waco of cult leader David Koresh and about 80 of his followers, and was influenced by news accounts blaming federal agents.
The jury, which convicted McVeigh of the bombing last week, must decide whether he should be executed or get life in prison for the 1995 bombing.

The defence is expected to wrap up its case on Wednesday and put McVeigh's father, Bill, on the stand to plead for his son's life. "I think we'll end ours (case), sometime tomorrow," Jones said as he left the courthouse.

Jones told reporters that McVeigh will not take the stand. James Nichols, the brother of McVeigh's alleged co-conspirator Terry Nichols, will also not appear, another defence attorney said. Nichols will be tried separately later.
Prosecutors alleged McVeigh was so angered by the raid that he took revenge by bombing the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people and injuring hundreds.
Jones said the defence is not admitting to the bombing. "Of course, we're not admitting anything," Jones said. "We have to accept the jury's verdict at this stage," Jones told reporters.
Federal Judge Richard Matsch cautioned the jury that they were presented evidence about Waco in order to assess McVeigh's views and beliefs, not to retry the incident.

But the defence kept the focus on Waco all day, putting on the stand reporters who had written about it and playing an hour-long video, "Day 51, The True Story of Waco," featuring scenes of the fire that destroyed the cult compound and ended the 51-day siege.

The video, critical of the actions of federal agents at Waco, showed pictures of cult members who died in the fire, reminiscent of testimony during the penalty phase about victims in the Oklahoma bombing.
Survivors and relatives of bombing victims testified for 2- 1/2 heart-wrenching days about how their lives had been irrevocably changed by the bombing.

In another video a song was played aimed at evoking sympathy about the children who died at Waco. "Seventeen little children, also helpless and so small died a senseless death of gas and flame. How many names can you recall?" the song asked.
The government was widely criticised over Waco, but the incident became a rallying cry for the extreme right wing.

In a rare moment the jurors heard McVeigh's own words, as the judge read aloud in a matter-of-fact voice a signed affidavit acknowledging he had read and seen a variety of magazine articles and videos about the Waco siege.
In the affidavit, McVeigh said he read many articles in Soldier of Fortune magazine, a publication popular among soldiers, survivalists and gun enthusiasts.

Defence attorneys tried to show the human side of McVeigh, putting on the stand in previous sessions boyhood friends, family and old army buddies who portrayed McVeigh as a smart and friendly youngster and a model soldier.

When the defence wraps up its case it is expected to focus on McVeigh's honourable service in the military and the fact that he has no criminal record. The defence may also try to use as a mitigating factor McVeigh's conviction that the United States was turning into a police state.

However, in a court filing prosecutors have objected to some proposed instructions to the jury that the defence wants, such as his belief that the government was responsible for the deaths at Waco and the possibility that if McVeigh is sentenced to life in prison he may someday disclose the full story of the bombing.
